intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note says why a slide matters, how to remember it and where practice slips. Do the exercises with your own programme in mind, and ask of every result whether it measures access or control.

sections.title: What Is Women's Economic Empowerment?
sections.big_idea: Empowerment is the power to **decide and act** on economic matters, so a job or an income is only half of it.
in_plain_words: Women's economic empowerment is the process by which women gain the power to make and act on economic decisions, expand their choices and benefit from the results, on terms they value. Naila Kabeer's framework gives it three dimensions: resources, agency and achievements. Each depends on the one before, and none is enough alone. A woman who hands over her wages, or whose account someone else operates, shows a positive income result with no change in power.

Choice is the heart of it. Kabeer ties empowerment to a movement from denial to the ability to make strategic life choices, such as whether to work, marry or move. Agency takes many forms, including bargaining and everyday resistance, and surveys capture few of them. **Employment, work, income and empowerment are four different things**, and programme reports often use them as if they were one.

nodes.label: Agency
nodes.sub: power to define goals and act

nodes.label: Achievements
nodes.sub: what she can be and do

key_terms.meaning: The process of gaining power to make and act on economic decisions and benefit from them.
The power to define goals and act on them, from decisions to collective action.
Reported satisfaction within unjust limits, so consent is not always free choice.
A major life decision such as whether to work, marry or move.
Whether she, and no one else, decides how her income or asset is used.

worked_example.title: Weak or strong indicator?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a programme report lists three results. Sort each as a weak indicator or a better one, using Kabeer's dimensions.
steps: 'Accounts opened' is a resource indicator and a weak one. The better version is an account she operates herself.
'Women attended a meeting' is an agency indicator and a weak one. The better version is a decision that changed because of her.
'Household income rose' is an achievement indicator and a weak one. The better version is her own consumption and health improving.
Report the stronger column, and say so when only the weak column is available.
worked_example.answer: All three are weak. Each needs its better version: operation, a changed decision, and her own outcomes.

mistakes: Counting an account as empowerment when someone else operates it. That is access without control.
Reporting an employment result as an empowerment result. The difference costs one word and changes the claim.
Reading survey decision questions as the whole of agency. Bargaining and everyday resistance are rarely measured.
Treating a woman's stated satisfaction as proof of free choice, when it may be an adaptive preference.

recall.q: Name Kabeer's three dimensions.
recall.a: Resources, agency and achievements.

recall.q: Why does Kabeer say people who already exercise a great deal of choice are not empowered?
recall.a: Because they were never disempowered in the first place. Empowerment is a process of change from denial of choice.

recall.q: Give two forms of agency from the deck.
recall.a: Decision-making, bargaining and negotiation within the household, resistance and everyday subversion, or collective action.

recall.q: What does the 'Income' row say the term does not tell you?
recall.a: Whether she controls it.

recall.q: Why do single-dimension programmes underperform?
recall.a: The economic, social and relational dimensions reinforce each other, so a woman who owns land but cannot travel to market has an asset she cannot deploy.

sections.title: Why WEE Matters
sections.big_idea: Lead with **rights**, then offer returns as a second argument, and plan for the resistance that a shift in power will meet.
in_plain_words: The case for women's economic autonomy begins with rights: constitutional guarantees in Articles 14 to 16, equal pay in the Code on Wages, CEDAW ratified in 1993 and property rights under the 2005 amendment. A rights case is more durable, because an argument resting on returns can be defeated by evidence about returns while one resting on entitlement cannot. The development case is real too. Evidence on children's nutrition and schooling is reasonably consistent, while aggregate growth estimates vary with assumptions.

'Smart economics' used the returns argument to open funding and reach finance ministries, and it cost something. It can treat women as a means and add paid work on top of unchanged care. The mature position holds rights first and returns alongside. **Power is partly redistributive**, so more agency for women can mean less control for men, and backlash is documented. Plan for it and drop the assumption that everyone gains.

left.title: Rights case
items: Use with a court or movement

diagram.caption: hold both, in order, with rights first

key_terms.meaning: The women's rights convention that India ratified in 1993.
The argument that women's participation is an efficient means to growth.
Value women for their returns to others instead of as rights-holders.
Assuming more power for women threatens no one.
Resistance in the household, market or institution to women's gains.

worked_example.title: Match the argument to the audience
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: you must brief three audiences on one WEE programme. Choose the lead argument for each, using the deck's table.
steps: A rights-based donor, a court or a movement: lead with rights and entitlement.
A finance ministry or corporate partner: lead with development returns, and cite source, year and scenario for any GDP figure.
Most other audiences: give both, in order, rights first.
For every audience, name the redistribution in the design and plan engaging men and a referral route.
worked_example.answer: Rights for donors, courts and movements, returns for ministries and companies, and both in order for the rest.

mistakes: Quoting a GDP-gain figure with no source, year or scenario. It is the easiest claim in the field to dismiss.
Letting the returns case replace the rights case, which leaves the argument open to defeat by returns evidence.
Treating a rise in paid work as improvement when care work has not fallen and the day has lengthened.
Assuming nobody loses from women's gains. Control shifts, and someone bears a cost.

recall.q: Which instruments does the deck give as the rights basis?
recall.a: Articles 14, 15 and 16, the Code on Wages 2019, CEDAW (ratified 1993) and the Hindu Succession Amendment 2005.

recall.q: What does the deck say is the claim of 'smart economics'?
recall.a: That gender equality, and women's economic participation in particular, is an efficient means to development and growth.

recall.q: What is the 'efficient mother' risk?
recall.a: Programmes route benefits through her to children and treat her as a means to development.

recall.q: What should accompany any GDP-gain estimate?
recall.a: The source, the year and the scenario.

recall.q: Which tools does the deck suggest to plan for backlash?
recall.a: Engaging men, do-no-harm monitoring and a referral route.

sections.title: The Unpaid Care Economy
sections.big_idea: Care is **the central constraint** on women's economic options, and no WEE intervention works without asking what it does to her time.
in_plain_words: Cooking, cleaning, fetching water and fuel, and caring for children, the sick and the elderly sustain every household, and they are mostly absent from GDP. Growing food for your household counts, while cooking it does not, because the boundary falls between goods and services. India's Time Use Survey (2019 and 2024) shows women spending several times as many minutes as men on unpaid domestic work, and it makes the uncounted portion measurable.

The care load starts a loop: less time for paid work, part-time or home-based work, lower earnings, weaker bargaining power and less ability to renegotiate care. Moser's triple role adds community work to productive and reproductive work. The 4 Rs give the toolkit: recognise, reduce, redistribute, represent. Missing public services such as water, LPG and anganwadis drive much of the burden, so **quantify the time returned** when arguing for them.

diagram.caption: the loop repeats until the care side changes

key_terms.meaning: Care and domestic services provided without payment, excluded from GDP.
Moser's productive, reproductive and community work.
Recognise, reduce, redistribute, represent.
NSO survey, run in 2019 and 2024, that measures unpaid work.
Heavy unpaid tasks such as water and fuel collection that services can reduce.

worked_example.title: Does the programme lengthen her day?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a woman spends 4 hours on paid work and 5 hours on unpaid care. A programme lifts her paid work to 7 hours and leaves care unchanged.
steps: Total work before: 4 + 5 = 9 hours.
Total work after: 7 + 5 = 12 hours.
Change in the working day: 12 − 9 = 3 hours longer.
Earnings rose but care did not fall, so the programme added to her day.
worked_example.answer: Her working day grows by 3 hours, so the gain in paid work comes with a cost in time.

mistakes: Adding paid work with no change to care, which deepens exhaustion without empowerment.
Treating infrastructure as a general development matter when each missing service costs women daily hours.
Funding only 'reduce' and expecting a change in who does the work. Reduce lowers the total and leaves the share unchanged.
Setting an activity schedule without reading the time-use tables for your own state.

recall.q: Which care work is counted in GDP according to the table?
recall.a: Subsistence food production, because it is a good. Cooking, cleaning, childcare and eldercare are not.

recall.q: What are Moser's three roles?
recall.a: Productive, reproductive and community.

recall.q: What does the 4 Rs framework add to Elson's three Rs?
recall.a: Represent, and the ILO also adds Reward, extending it to five.

recall.q: Which missing services does the deck list as costing women hours?
recall.a: Piped water, LPG, electricity and a functioning anganwadi.

recall.q: What are the four design questions at the end of the section?
recall.a: Does it reduce her unpaid load, does it redistribute care, have we costed her time and is childcare provided?

sections.title: Women's Labour Force Participation
sections.big_idea: India's female participation rate is low, fell for years and has recently risen, and **how you count decides the answer**.
in_plain_words: LFPR is the share of the working-age population that is employed or actively seeking work. India's rate for women is among the world's lowest. It fell through the 2000s and 2010s as incomes and girls' education rose, and PLFS data show a rise since around 2017-18. That rise is driven substantially by rural self-employment and unpaid family labour, so look at composition before reading the rate.

Six explanations compete: the income effect, unpaid care, norms and status, missing jobs, safety and mobility, and measurement. Debate is about weights, since no single cause explains it. Counting matters because women's work is easily missed. A bare 'did you work last week' catches recognised paid work, while a probed activity list or time-use diary catches far more. Most working women are informal, so **formal-employment entitlements reach a small minority**.

diagram.caption: no single cause: all three at once

key_terms.meaning: Share of working-age people employed or actively seeking work.
Participation falls as income rises, then rises with education and good jobs.
One definition of working; it differs from current weekly status.
Work without a contract, social security or stable pay.
An organisation of informal women workers.

worked_example.title: How wording moves the rate
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a village has 1,000 women of working age. Survey A asks 'did you work last week' and finds 300 employed or seeking work. Survey B uses a probed activity list and finds 360.
steps: The difference is 36 − 30 = 6 percentage points, from question wording alone.
State which series and which question you used before comparing across sources.
worked_example.answer: 30% against 36%: a 6-point gap created by measurement, with the same women.

mistakes: Comparing female LFPR across surveys without checking definitions. NSS and PLFS are not identical series.
Reading the recent PLFS rise as a rise in good work without looking at unpaid family labour.
Citing a national average and skipping the rural and urban split. Always disaggregate by location and social group.
Designing around employer-linked benefits when most working women are informal.

recall.q: What are the three parts of India's participation puzzle?
recall.a: The level is low, it fell as incomes and education rose, and it has recently risen.

recall.q: What are the stages of the U-shape?
recall.a: Low income with high participation, rising income with a dip, and higher education plus good jobs with a rise.

recall.q: Name three of the six explanations for low participation.
recall.a: Any three of: income effect, unpaid care, norms and status, missing jobs, safety and mobility, measurement.

recall.q: What does a time-use diary capture?
recall.a: Nearly all of women's work, against recognised paid work only for a bare question.

recall.q: What is the rural-urban difference in rights-based work?
recall.a: Rural women have MGNREGA, and urban women have no equivalent.

sections.title: Pay Gaps & Occupational Segregation
sections.big_idea: The pay gap is **structural**: it is built from segregation, devalued care work, the motherhood penalty and discrimination.
in_plain_words: The gender pay gap is the difference between men's and women's earnings as a percentage of men's. It combines different jobs, hours and experience with unequal pay for like work. A raw gap and an adjusted gap answer different questions, and the commonest reporting error is quoting one as the other. The 'explained' portion is not innocent, because occupation, experience and hours are themselves shaped by gender and care.

Horizontal segregation puts women in lower-paid fields, and the care penalty finds that work coded as caring pays less after controlling for skill. Vertical segregation shows as a glass ceiling, a sticky floor and a broken first rung. The motherhood penalty has no matching fatherhood penalty. The Equal Remuneration Act is now inside the Code on Wages, but enforcement fails in informal work. **Report the gap by grade**, and favour pay transparency.

diagram.note: each part is shaped by gender and care, so report raw and adjusted gaps together

key_terms.meaning: Unadjusted difference in earnings, right for what women earn relative to men.
Gap after controlling for job, hours and experience, right for like-for-like pay.
Women and men clustered in different occupations and sectors.
The first step into management, where representation drops most.
Earnings and employment loss after having children.

worked_example.title: Compute a raw gap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: men in a firm earn 20,000 a month on average and women earn 15,000.
steps: Gap as a share of men's earnings: 5,000 ÷ 20,000 = 25%.
This is a raw gap: it says what women earn relative to men.
To speak of discrimination, you would also need an adjusted gap with job, hours and experience held equal.
worked_example.answer: A raw gap of 25%, which should be reported with the adjusted figure and what each includes.

mistakes: Quoting an adjusted gap alone. It understates disadvantage because it removes segregation from the estimate.
Reporting one overall gap. The drivers differ by tier and a small average can hide a large gap at promotion level.
Telling women to lean in or negotiate better. The gap persists after controlling for the choices in question.
Fixing segregation only by moving women into male jobs, with no revaluing of feminised work.

recall.q: Define the gender pay gap.
recall.a: The difference between men's and women's earnings, usually as a percentage of men's earnings.

recall.q: What are the three patterns of vertical segregation?
recall.a: Glass ceiling, sticky floor and broken rung.

recall.q: Which drivers dominate at entry, mid and senior level?
recall.a: Occupational sorting at entry, the motherhood penalty at mid level, and vertical segregation at senior level.

recall.q: Which instrument has the best evidence for reducing the motherhood penalty?
recall.a: Non-transferable parental leave for fathers.

recall.q: Which law mandates equal pay and where is it now?
recall.a: The Equal Remuneration Act 1976, subsumed into the Code on Wages 2019.

sections.title: Assets, Land & Property
sections.big_idea: Assets shift power more durably than income, so **whose name is on the paper** is the intervention.
in_plain_words: Income can be handed over and spent, while assets such as land, a house or livestock give security, collateral, status and a fallback. Ownership is among the strongest correlates of women's bargaining power, largely because it raises the outside option. Women operate only a small share of agricultural land despite doing much of the farm work, and entitlements keyed to the land record leave women without title outside crop insurance, credit and subsidies.

Custom gave sons land and daughters dowry. The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 made daughters coparceners by birth, and Vineeta Sharma (2020) settled that this does not depend on the father being alive in 2005. In practice the most common outcome is a claim never made, so **collective backing changes the cost of asserting the right**. Titling programmes need checks: joint titles often limit sale or mortgage, and some women do not know they are named.

key_terms.meaning: A member with a birthright in ancestral property; daughters since 2005.
What she could do if the relationship ended, which shapes bargaining.
Both names on the deed; it can limit sale, lease or mortgage.
Correcting land records after inheritance or transfer.
Farming in which women do more field labour as men migrate.

worked_example.title: Audit a housing scheme allotment
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a scheme allots 100 houses and says it 'favours women's ownership'. Decide what to check before calling it a WEE result, using the deck's four questions.
steps: Is it in her own name? A house in the husband's name is a household asset.
Is the record updated? If the paper does not follow, the right is lost.
Can she use it as collateral? A joint title may prevent it.
Does she know she owns it? Hand over the document in person and explain what it means.
worked_example.answer: Count a house as her asset only when the name, record, collateral use and her awareness are all confirmed.

mistakes: Treating access indicators as power. Financial access has neared parity while control has not.
Assuming awareness of the 2005 right is enough. Most unclaimed rights are unclaimed under family pressure.
Forgetting that the Act covers Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, so other personal laws apply to other families.
Counting a joint title as full ownership when the owner cannot sell or mortgage without the other.

recall.q: What did the 2005 amendment do?
recall.a: It made daughters equal coparceners by birth in ancestral property, on the same footing as sons.

recall.q: What did Vineeta Sharma (2020) settle?
recall.a: That a daughter's coparcenary right is by birth and does not depend on the father being alive in 2005.

recall.q: Why are women farmers invisible to extension and credit?
recall.a: Entitlements are keyed to the land record, and titles remain overwhelmingly in men's names.

recall.q: Name two obstacles to claiming and their remedies.
recall.a: Low awareness (rights literacy), out-of-date records (mutation), family pressure (collective support, legal aid), litigation cost (free legal services).

recall.q: Which quotation opens the section's case for assets?
recall.a: Bina Agarwal: the gender gap in command over property is the single most important economic factor affecting women's situation.

sections.title: Financial Inclusion
sections.big_idea: Access is the start and **control is the goal**: measure active, independent use of an account, and drop accounts opened as the headline.
in_plain_words: A bank account gives a place to keep money out of others' reach, a route for wages and benefits, a credit history and a foothold for enterprise, but only if it is hers. Ask who operates the account, who holds the passbook and who knows the PIN. India's self-help groups pool savings, lend internally and later link to banks, with group reputation replacing collateral. The track record is the security, so a group linked before it exists defaults more.

Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and mobile enable direct transfers, though many accounts are dormant, authentication errors fall hardest on the people the transfer should reach, and the digital gender gap in phones limits reach. Microcredit shows promise and peril: rigorous evaluations generally find modest effects on business activity and little on women's empowerment. **Empowerment is not a heavier loan**, so measure whether the debt is manageable.

diagram.caption: the SHG-bank linkage sequence cannot be shortcut

key_terms.meaning: A group of 10 to 20 women who save, lend to each other and link to a bank.
SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, developed through NABARD from the early 1990s.
Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and mobile, enabling direct benefit transfers.
An account opened but rarely used or controlled by the woman.
Women's lower phone ownership, data access and independent use.

worked_example.title: Size an SHG's own fund
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an SHG has 15 members and each saves 100 a month. Work out the fund the group controls.
steps: Monthly pool: 15 × 100 = 1,500.
This fund is the group's own capital and the base for internal lending.
Only after this track record does the group seek bank linkage, which then lends at scale without collateral.
worked_example.answer: A fund of 18,000 in a year, built by saving before borrowing.

mistakes: Counting accounts opened as financial inclusion, when none of the four benefits arrive if a husband operates it.
Linking a group to a bank before it has a savings and lending record.
Using the phone number on a woman's account for sensitive messages without asking whose phone it is.
Reading loan uptake as an empowerment indicator when loans are used by men and repaid by women.

recall.q: What distinguishes an SHG from a microfinance client group?
recall.a: Saving comes before borrowing, which builds the group's own capital.

recall.q: What are the three questions that separate access from control?
recall.a: Who operates the account, who holds the passbook and who knows the PIN.

recall.q: What did the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis of 2010 show?
recall.a: That credit pushed without livelihoods or protection can trap borrowers.

recall.q: What is Kudumbashree's distinctive feature?
recall.a: State-wide neighbourhood groups linked institutionally to local government.

recall.q: What should replace 'accounts opened' as a measure?
recall.a: Active, independent use of the account.

sections.title: Entrepreneurship & Enterprise
sections.big_idea: Enterprise is **embedded in the same web** of assets, mobility, norms and care, so credit alone rarely lifts a women-led firm.
in_plain_words: Women own a minority of India's enterprises, and most are micro and own-account firms in tailoring, food, beauty and petty trade, which fit restricted mobility and a care load. Most women entrepreneurs are nearer the necessity end than the opportunity end. Policy designed for the second group can miss the first, so segment before designing. Barriers compound: credit, mobility, networks, markets, care and time, skills and confidence.

Credit gaps trace to the asset gap, and schemes such as MUDRA and Stand-Up India widen collateral-light lending, though documents, bank discretion and awareness still decide take-up. Women cluster in low-margin nodes of the value chain, and collectives such as FPOs and SEWA cooperatives help them move up. The strongest evidence favours bundles: capital with skills, mentoring, market links and care support. **Market linkage is the most consistently missing element.**

diagram.caption: value chain nodes, top first: margin sits above women

key_terms.meaning: Starts a tiny venture because no suitable wage job exists.
Spots a market gap and chooses to build a growth business.
Farmer producer organisation, a collective for aggregating and selling.
A scheme that widens collateral-light lending.
Asset, stipend, training and savings bundled, pioneered by BRAC.

worked_example.title: Segment two entrepreneurs
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: Meena sews at home because no wage job is available. Priya has spotted a market gap and plans to hire staff. Decide what each needs.
steps: Meena started because there was no suitable wage job and she works at home around care: necessity-driven.
What helps Meena is reducing the binding constraint, such as childcare, timing and local markets.
Priya is opportunity-driven: expansion intent, located where the market is.
What helps Priya is capital and market access.
worked_example.answer: Meena needs a constraint reduced, Priya needs capital and market access. One programme serves neither well.

mistakes: Offering training and loans designed for the opportunity column to necessity entrepreneurs, who cannot use them.
Addressing only credit and leaving mobility, markets and care in place.
Increasing output at the bottom of the chain, when the return sits higher up.
Funding production capacity with no buyer, which produces unsold stock.

recall.q: Name three sectors where women-led firms cluster.
recall.a: Tailoring, food, beauty or petty trade.

recall.q: Which earlier section does the credit barrier trace to?
recall.a: Section 6, the asset gap.

recall.q: What do collectives such as SHG federations and producer companies pool?
recall.a: Capital, risk, market scale and bargaining power; a registered producer company is also a legal entity.

recall.q: What does the graduation approach bundle?
recall.a: An asset, a stipend or cash, training and coaching, and savings.

recall.q: What does a good enterprise programme address alongside capital?
recall.a: Care, mobility, networks and markets.

sections.title: Agency, Norms & Decision-Making
sections.big_idea: The household and the norm sit **between the resource and the outcome**, which is why economic gains produce uneven empowerment.
in_plain_words: Economics long modelled the household as one decision-maker. In reality members have different preferences and unequal power, and a person's fallback position shapes their bargaining power. Four things strengthen her hand: income she controls, assets in her name, support from her natal family and a group behind her. Decision indicators need careful reading, since 'joint' can mask male dominance and 'alone' may mean abandonment.

Norms are unwritten rules sustained by approval, and they persist even when people privately disagree, because each thinks others approve. Gains can trigger backlash, so do no harm: engage men, avoid public exposure of amounts and keep a referral route. Mobility and safety are economic infrastructure. Moving from unpaid to paid work brings gains and costs, so **track total time, control of earnings and decent work**. Norm work is slow, hard to attribute and the least funded.

diagram.caption: four sources, one mechanism: the outside option

key_terms.meaning: Negotiation over resources, labour and consumption within a household.
What a person could get outside the household.
An unwritten rule sustained by social approval and sanction.
Private rejection of a norm and public compliance because others seem to approve.
Never leave a woman more exposed for having taken part.

worked_example.title: Read a decision indicator
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a survey finds most women answer 'decides jointly' on large purchases, and 10% say 'decides alone'. Interpret the result using the deck's table.
steps: 'Decides alone' may indicate abandonment and so may say little about power. Do not read it as success.
'Decides jointly' is the largest group and the hardest to interpret, because it may mask male dominance.
'Someone else decides' is clear.
Add one qualitative probe on how the last major purchase was actually decided, and the item on her own earnings.
worked_example.answer: The index alone cannot show empowerment. The probe and the earnings item give the fuller picture.

mistakes: Treating the household as a single mind and targeting it, when targeting the woman is different.
Publicising amounts a woman has earned, when visibility raises backlash risk.
Using women-only sessions for norm change. Men and families hold the other half of the norm.
Making men the visible voice of the work, which repeats the pattern the work aims to change.

recall.q: What does the unitary household model assume?
recall.a: One set of preferences, pooled income, efficient allocation and that targeting the household is enough.

recall.q: Why does SHG membership show an empowerment effect even with small loans?
recall.a: The group changes her outside option.

recall.q: What is the most informative single decision item?
recall.a: Whether she decides on her own earnings.

recall.q: What should be tracked when a woman moves into paid work?
recall.a: Total time use, control over earnings and the quality of the work.

recall.q: What is a cheap intervention when many privately reject a norm?
recall.a: Publicising the true distribution of private opinion.

sections.title: Legal Rights & the Enabling Environment
sections.big_idea: Rights make gains durable, and the frontier is **claiming mechanisms that reach the informal majority**.
in_plain_words: Individual gains can be reversed by one household decision, while a statutory entitlement with a working claiming mechanism cannot. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 extended paid leave from 12 to 26 weeks and required creches in larger establishments, though it excludes informal workers and the employer-borne cost may affect hiring. The PoSH Act 2013 requires Internal Committees and Local Committees for the informal sector, and implementation is patchy. MGNREGA carried gender provisions that can be checked on muster rolls, and the deck records its replacement from 1 July 2026.

Social protection instruments each have enrolment conditions, and a woman without documents in her own name misses several at once. In each case the right exists and the mechanism does not reach her, which is a different problem from a weak law. Protections can also backfire if the cost falls on employers, so **socialise the cost or make the requirement universal**. Programmes should connect to an entitlement, build a claiming route, reach informal workers and survive exit.

diagram.caption: each sets a floor and promises no outcome

key_terms.meaning: The 2013 Act requiring employers to prevent and redress sexual harassment.
The workplace body PoSH requires above a size threshold.
District body extending PoSH to small units and the informal sector.
Public MGNREGA record used to monitor women's share and wages.
A registry that is a route towards covering informal workers.

worked_example.title: Check two statutory numbers
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a worksite has 600 person-days of MGNREGA work in a month, and the Maternity Act's extension is from 12 to 26 weeks.
steps: Minimum women's share: 600 ÷ 3 = 200 person-days.
Read the muster roll: if women's days are below 200, the provision is not met.
Extra maternity leave: 26 − 12 = 14 weeks.
Remember both are floors that depend on enforcement and coverage.
worked_example.answer: At least 200 of 600 person-days for women, and 14 more weeks of leave for those covered.

mistakes: Assuming the Maternity Act covers most working women. It covers the small formal sector.
Advocating a higher legal floor when the claiming mechanism does not work locally.
Leaving women out of social protection by ignoring that they may lack documents in their own name.
Weakening a protection to fix hiring bias, when the fix is to socialise the cost.

recall.q: Which legal frame replaced the Equal Remuneration Act?
recall.a: The Code on Wages, 2019.

recall.q: What did the 2017 Maternity amendment change?
recall.a: Paid leave rose from 12 to 26 weeks for eligible women, with creches in larger establishments.

recall.q: What are MGNREGA's gender provisions?
recall.a: At least a third of work for women, equal wages, worksite creches and work close to home.

recall.q: Where does PoSH implementation usually fail?
recall.a: Internal Committees not constituted or inactive, Local Committees rarely functional, annual reports not filed.

recall.q: What four tests end the section?
recall.a: Does it connect to an entitlement, build a claiming route, reach informal workers and survive our exit?

sections.title: Measuring WEE & What Works
sections.big_idea: Measure **control as well as access**, at the individual level, and favour bundles over single instruments.
in_plain_words: Empowerment is a process inside people's lives, so any indicator is a proxy, and honest practice names the proxy and what it misses. Measure at more than one point, ask what she values and watch for response shift. The strong indicator is an asset in her own name, a decision about her own earnings and her own nutrition, and the weak substitutes are household-level figures that hide intra-household inequality. The WEAI, developed by IFPRI, USAID and OPHI, covers production, resources, income, leadership and time, and interviews both a woman and a man in the household.

On what works, cash transfers help consumption while agency gains vary, assets in her name shift power more durably, credit alone is mixed, and graduation bundles are among the most consistent. Bundles cost more per participant, which is a real budget trade-off. Disaggregate by caste, class, disability, marital status and location. If you carry one idea, carry this: **almost every overstated empowerment claim is an access figure reported as a control finding.**

key_terms.meaning: Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index, comparing women with men in a household.
Combine economic, agency and control measures with qualitative voice.
A programme changes what a woman considers normal, so an answer means something new at endline.
A bundle of asset, cash, coaching and savings.
Caste, class, disability and other axes that compound constraints.

worked_example.title: The budget trade-off
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a programme has a budget of 600,000. A single component costs 3,000 per participant and a graduation bundle costs 12,000.
steps: Single component: 600,000 ÷ 3,000 = 200 participants.
Bundle: 600,000 ÷ 12,000 = 50 participants.
The bundle reaches 150 fewer people: 200 − 50 = 150.
The evidence suggests the bundle gives larger and more durable effects, so state which choice you made and why.
worked_example.answer: 200 participants with a single component or 50 with a bundle, a choice to state openly.

mistakes: Using a household measure for a claim about women. A household figure cannot support it.
Imposing a definition of empowerment instead of asking what she values.
Reporting an average that hides the most marginalised women or widens gaps between women.
Choosing indicators that cannot move within the programme horizon.

recall.q: Which dimension does the WEAI include that most measures omit?
recall.a: Time.

recall.q: What does the evidence say about credit alone?
recall.a: Modest business effects and little on empowerment; it can over-indebt without support.

recall.q: What is the first principle in the five-point summary?
recall.a: Rights first: the case for WEE is justice as well as returns.

recall.q: Which question does the 'control over access' principle become?
recall.a: Whose name, and who decides?

recall.q: Why disaggregate?
recall.a: A programme that raises the average can bypass the most marginalised or widen gaps between women.

notes.2: Read the agenda as a chain of constraints: care first, then work, pay, assets, finance and enterprise, then agency and law, then measurement. Each section depends on the earlier ones. If you have little time, take **care, agency and measurement**, which the roadmap slide says carry most of what changes a design.
notes.4: Split the definition in two. Resources answer 'does she have it?' and agency answers 'can she decide and act?' Both halves must be present. Use the table as a screening test on any project report: whenever you read 'she earns', ask **who decides and who operates the account**.
notes.5: Memorise the three words in order: resources, agency, achievements. They are sequential, and none is enough alone. The table gives a stronger indicator for each. Next time you review a log frame, check whether it reports only the **weak column**, since that column is why participants may not recognise a claimed success.
notes.6: Kabeer's point is that empowerment needs a prior denial of choice, so a snapshot of someone already powerful shows nothing. Look at the last row: a choice with no viable alternative is no choice. That is why **enabling conditions matter as much as attitudes**. Compare strategic choices (work, marry, move) with everyday ones.
notes.7: Agency has four forms, and surveys capture only the first and last. Bargaining and everyday resistance happen quietly. Qualitative work finds them. Keep the warning on adaptive preferences in mind: **voiced consent is not always free choice**, so a woman reporting satisfaction may be adjusting to limits.
notes.8: Four words that programme documents use as if they were one. The first table says what each captures and the second says what each leaves out. Test your own reports. If you measured employment, call it employment. A single word costs little and **separates an accurate claim from an inflated one**.
notes.9: Three dimensions reinforce each other: economic, social and relational. The links are real but never automatic. The land example is easy to remember: a woman who owns land but cannot travel to market has an asset she cannot use. This is the reasoning behind **bundled programmes** in Section 11.
notes.10: The roadmap puts a question to each section. Care asks what her day is already full of, and measurement asks how we would know. The order is deliberate. **Care comes first because it constrains everything after it**, and measurement comes last because it depends on knowing what to measure.
notes.12: Lead with rights. The table lists four instruments you can cite: Articles 14 to 16, the Code on Wages, CEDAW and the Hindu Succession Amendment. A rights case is more durable because **an argument resting on returns can be defeated by evidence about returns**, while one resting on entitlement cannot.
notes.13: The development case is real but its evidence has different strength by claim. Children's nutrition and schooling are reasonably consistent, while growth effects are model-dependent. When you cite it, **separate direction from magnitude**. Quote a number without its source and method, and a critic will dismiss the argument as a whole.
notes.14: The chart is illustrative, so read it for direction only. The table shows why published estimates differ: the counterfactual and the time horizon. When you cite a GDP gain, give **source, year and scenario**. A bare number is the easiest claim in this field to dismiss.
notes.15: 'Smart economics' says invest in women because it pays. The table shows both sides: it opened funding and reached finance ministries, and it made the case instrumental. Use it where it works, such as with a finance ministry, but keep **the rights argument as the position you actually hold**.
notes.16: Four critiques, each with a concrete risk. The third has been documented repeatedly: participation rises, care work does not fall and total hours increase. So **measure total time as well as paid work**. A programme that raises earnings and lengthens the day may not have helped.
notes.17: Hold both arguments, in order: rights first, returns alongside. The table says which audience gets which. Calling the returns case a bonus protects you from the failure on the slide, which is letting the second argument replace the first. Then **the case can be defeated by returns evidence**.
notes.18: 'Win-win' assumes nobody loses. The table's right-hand column says otherwise: control shifts, backlash is documented and someone bears a cost. Plan for it. The bottom paragraph lists three tools: **engaging men, do-no-harm monitoring and a referral route** for women who meet resistance.
notes.20: Unpaid care is real work that is mostly absent from GDP. The table also shows the odd boundary: growing food for your household counts, cooking it does not. The line separates goods from services. Remember that **India's Time Use Survey (2019 and 2024)** makes the uncounted portion measurable.
notes.21: The chart is illustrative, but the pattern from the Time Use Survey is firm: women spend several times as many minutes on unpaid domestic work as men. Two national rounds let you track change. Before you fix an activity schedule, **read the tables for your own state**.
notes.22: Follow the four boxes as a loop: heavy care load, less time for paid work, part-time or home-based work, lower earnings and weaker bargaining, and back to the start. Because of the loop, **care is the central constraint**. Raising earning opportunities alone leaves the first link untouched.
notes.23: Moser's three roles are productive, reproductive and community. Only the first is usually paid and counted. For each project ask which role you are adding to. The third is the one programmes create most casually, through a committee or volunteer post, and **it is unpaid by design**.
notes.24: Recognise, reduce, redistribute and represent form the care toolkit. The table gives an instrument and a typical failure for each. Reduce is easiest to fund and limited, since it lowers the total and leaves **who does it unchanged**. Note that Elson's framework began with three Rs and the ILO extended it.
notes.25: Much unpaid time compensates for missing public services. Each row converts a missing service into hours: water, fuel, electricity, anganwadi. That makes infrastructure a women's economic intervention. When you argue for it, **quantify the time returned**, because that is the argument that reaches a planning department.
notes.26: This slide is a bridge. Here care is the binding constraint on women's economic options, and the Care Economy 101 deck treats care as a subject. Use the table to decide what to read where. If care is central to your work, read both, and **take measurement and financing from the other deck**.
notes.27: Use the four questions as a design gate: does it reduce her load, redistribute care, cost her time and provide childcare? Any 'no' means you are adding to her day. A concrete handle is worksite creches under MGNREGA, whose absence is **monitorable and actionable**.
notes.29: India's puzzle has three parts: the level is low, it fell as incomes and education rose, and it has recently risen. Each part is contested. The rise since 2017-18 is driven substantially by rural self-employment and unpaid family labour. **Look at composition before reading the rate**.
notes.30: The chart is schematic: a long decline and then a recent rise. Definitions drive levels, so two credible sources can report different numbers for the same year. Whenever you compare, state **which survey and which status** you are using. Without it, the comparison cannot be read.
notes.31: Learn the U-shape as three stages: women work out of necessity at low income, withdraw from drudgery as income rises, and re-enter for education and white-collar jobs. India may be near the bottom. The policy question is whether the **upturn arrives automatically** or needs jobs that are scarce today.
notes.32: Six explanations compete, and the debate is about weights. The first table names each mechanism and the second says what would test it. The last row is the one you can act on: **better questions in your own baseline** will change what you record about women's work.
notes.33: How you ask decides what you count. Move down the table from a bare 'did you work last week' to a time-use diary and the estimate rises. Part of the recent PLFS rise reflects better capture. **Always check the definition** before reading a participation figure.
notes.34: Most working women are informal, so entitlements built around formal employment reach a small minority. Read the table from left to right: no contract means no enforceable terms, no employer of record means no maternity benefit. This is why **universal or residence-based provision** matters more than employer-linked provision.
notes.35: Rural and urban women face different realities, so always disaggregate. Rural participation is higher but much of it is unpaid family labour. Urban women lack a rights-based work guarantee. Note the parenthesis: the deck records that **MGNREGA was replaced from 1 July 2026**, so check which scheme applies.
notes.36: The takeaway lists five components and what would change each. No single lever moves the rate. Hold it as a labour-demand problem, a care problem, a norms problem and a measurement problem together. Locally, the fourth row is most actionable: **what jobs exist within safe reach**?
notes.38: Define the gap as a percentage of men's earnings. It combines different jobs, hours, experience and unequal pay for like work. The commonest reporting error is quoting a raw gap as if it were adjusted. Use **the raw gap for what women earn, and the adjusted gap for like-for-like discrimination**.
notes.39: The 'explained' part of a pay gap is not innocent. Occupation, experience and hours are all shaped by gender and by care. So controlling for them removes segregation from the estimate. **Report both numbers** and say what each includes, since an adjusted gap alone understates disadvantage.
notes.40: Horizontal segregation means women and men cluster in different jobs, and female-dominated jobs pay less than comparable work. The care penalty literature finds the same for men in these jobs. So closing the gap means **revaluing feminised work** as well as moving women into male-dominated occupations.
notes.41: Three vertical patterns: the glass ceiling at the top, the sticky floor at the bottom and the broken rung at the first promotion. The third is most open to intervention. **Track representation by grade** and not in aggregate, because an organisation can look acceptable overall with nobody above the first rung.
notes.42: The chart is illustrative: gaps persist across tiers and can widen at the top. The table ties each tier to a driver: sorting at entry, the motherhood penalty in the middle, vertical segregation at the top. Report the gap **by grade**, since the average hides where promotion decisions are made.
notes.43: The motherhood penalty is the earnings and employment loss after having children, with no matching fatherhood penalty. That asymmetry marks it as gendered. It works through dropping out, reduced hours, missed promotions and hiring bias. **Non-transferable parental leave for fathers** has the best evidence for reducing it.
notes.44: The Equal Remuneration Act 1976 now sits within the Code on Wages 2019. The table shows that enforcement depends on someone comparing pay, evidence and inspection. Most women work informally, so **no pay record exists to compare** and no inspection reaches them. Rights need teeth.
notes.45: The takeaway rejects the personal-choice explanation: the gap persists after controlling for the choices in question. Read the right column as what to stop doing, such as telling women to negotiate better. The mechanism to remember is **pay transparency**, because a gap that cannot be observed cannot be contested.
notes.47: Income can be handed over, while assets are harder to transfer and persist. The table contrasts the two. The bargaining reason is the outside option: **a credible ability to leave changes what can be negotiated inside**. The Agarwal quotation gives the strongest version.
notes.48: The bars are illustrative, but the documented reality is that women operate a small share of agricultural land despite doing much of the farm work. The last line carries a warning: access indicators improved dramatically and **tell you little about power**. Control has not neared parity.
notes.49: As men migrate, farming feminises, but titles stay in men's names. The table pairs what she does with what he holds. Entitlements are keyed to the land record, so a woman without a title is excluded from crop insurance, credit and subsidies. **Recognition as a farmer is the administrative precondition**.
notes.50: Inheritance is where the gap is made. Custom gave sons land and daughters dowry, a one-off transfer in place of a lasting asset. Since 2005 the law gives daughters a share, and only social pressure upholds the old pattern. Remember that unclaimed rights are mostly **unclaimed under family pressure**, so awareness alone is not enough.
notes.51: The 2005 amendment made daughters coparceners by birth, on the same footing as sons, including the right to demand partition. Vineeta Sharma (2020) settled that it does not depend on the father being alive in 2005. Check which personal law governs the family, because the Act covers **Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh** families.
notes.52: A strong law reaches the field slowly. The table links each obstacle to a remedy: rights literacy, record correction, collective support and legal aid, free legal services. The commonest outcome is a claim never made. So **collective backing changes the cost** of asserting the right.
notes.53: Titling puts women's names on paper. Use the table as a checklist: can she act without his consent, does the record reflect it, is the name hers or joint, are women named at all? Joint title often blocks sale or mortgage. Where possible choose **individual titling in her name**.
notes.54: Ask four questions of any asset transfer: is it in her name, is the record updated, can she use it as collateral and does she know she owns it? The fourth is a real finding in evaluations. **Hand over the document in person** and explain it.
notes.56: A bank account gives a place for money, a route for wages, a credit history and a foothold for enterprise, but only if she controls it. Three questions separate access from control: **who operates the account, who holds the passbook and who knows the PIN**. Opening an account counts for little by itself.
notes.57: An SHG is 10 to 20 women who save, lend internally and link to a bank. Sequence matters: saving before borrowing builds the group's own capital and separates an SHG from a microfinance client group. The meeting itself is a platform for **health, rights and collective action**, which makes it a WEE instrument.
notes.58: Follow the four boxes in order: save, lend internally, open a bank account, receive bank lending. Group reputation replaces collateral. The warning is about speed. The track record is the security, so **a group linked before it exists defaults more**. Do not shortcut the sequence.
notes.59: Three reference cases, each with a different strength: DAY-NRLM for national scale and federation, Kudumbashree for institutional links to local government, and SEWA for organising by occupation. Pick the case closest to your own design question. SEWA reaches workers **a village-based model cannot**.
notes.60: JAM can send wages and benefits straight into a woman's own account. It depends on the conditions in the right column: the account is hers and active, authentication works and she can reach a bank or agent. Failures fall hardest on the people the transfer should reach, and they are **under-reported by design**.
notes.61: Digital finance reaches women only if they own and control a phone. Each row in the table is a gap in ownership, independent use, data or literacy. If the phone is the husband's, 'her' account may not be hers. **Ask whose phone the number belongs to** before using it for anything sensitive.
notes.62: Read the table as paired columns of promise and peril. Small loans without collateral can become over-indebtedness, coercive collection or loans used by men and repaid by women. The third peril is the sharpest challenge to **treating loan uptake as an empowerment indicator**. Andhra Pradesh in 2010 was the warning.
notes.63: The takeaway reverses standard reporting. Replace accounts opened with active use, whose name with who operates it, loans disbursed with whether she chose the loan, and credit accessed with whether the debt is manageable. All four are **askable in a short survey module**. Empowerment is not a heavier loan.
notes.65: Women-led firms are mostly micro, own-account and often survivalist. The table links each feature to a consequence. The sector concentration reflects what is compatible with restricted mobility and a care load, so it is no preference finding. An enterprise programme that ignores mobility and care will produce **more of the same sectors**.
notes.66: Segment before you design. The necessity-driven entrepreneur starts because no wage job exists, and the opportunity-driven one sees a market gap. Most Indian women entrepreneurs sit near the necessity end. Programmes designed for the second column and delivered to the first create **training and loans that cannot be used**.
notes.67: Six barriers compound, so credit alone rarely lifts a firm. The second table traces each to an earlier section of the course. Use it as a diagnostic: a credit-only intervention addresses one row and leaves the others. That is **the argument for bundled programmes**.
notes.68: Women lack the collateral banks expect because they own little land. MUDRA, Stand-Up India and SHG linkage aim to widen collateral-light lending. The right column shows what still blocks take-up. The unglamorous work of **helping a woman assemble documents and approach the branch** often decides the outcome.
notes.69: Follow the chain from raw production to branding and retail. Women cluster at the low-margin nodes and men hold the higher ones. The return sits in moving up the chain, since more output at the bottom adds little. **Aggregation is the first node above production**, and collectives can reach it.
notes.70: Collectives pool capital, share risk, give market scale and offer a legal form. SEWA's cooperatives and Lijjat's papad network are the long-running Indian examples, and both took decades. The legal form matters: a registered producer company can **contract, borrow and sell** in ways an informal group cannot.
notes.71: A single cash grant or loan does little. Bundle capital with skills, mentoring, market links and care support. The graduation evidence is among the strongest in the field. Bundling costs more per participant, so the trade-off is real: **choose the components that match the binding constraint**.
notes.72: The takeaway says the best enterprise programmes are really WEE programmes. Use the table as a design checklist: care, mobility, networks and markets alongside capital. Market linkage is most often missing. Production capacity **without a buyer** produces unsold stock and loans repaid from other income.
notes.74: The unitary household model assumes one decision-maker, and the evidence against it is strong: transfers to women and to men produce different spending in the same households. That is the basis for targeting women. It also shows why **control matters more than receipt** when you measure.
notes.75: Four things strengthen a woman's hand: income she controls, assets in her name, support from her natal family and a group behind her. Bargaining models name the outside option as the mechanism. That explains why **SHG membership shows an empowerment effect** even where loans are small.
notes.76: NFHS-style questions ask who decides. The table shows the traps: deciding alone may mean abandonment, and deciding jointly may mask male dominance. The most informative single item is the woman's own earnings. Pair the index with a **qualitative probe on one recent decision**.
notes.77: A norm is an unwritten rule sustained by approval and sanction. The first row is pluralistic ignorance: many people privately disagree and comply because they think others approve. Then **publicising the true distribution of private opinion** can shift behaviour quickly, and it is one of the cheapest interventions.
notes.78: Backlash can follow gains in women's earning or autonomy. The table pairs each risk with a mitigation, such as engaging men early or avoiding public exposure of amounts. The evidence on direction is mixed, but the design response is the same. **Anticipate, monitor and have a referral route.**
notes.79: Treat mobility and safety as economic infrastructure. A job two hours away that she cannot safely reach is not an available job. The last row, no safe toilet at work, is specific and fixable. It is routinely omitted from **construction and informal work sites**.
notes.80: Norms and unpaid care are held collectively, so lasting change needs men, families and communities. The left column lists what to do with men: share care concretely, discuss what they gain, negotiate in the household, name the father's role. Guard against **men becoming the visible voice** of the work.
notes.81: Paid work is a goal and carries no automatic empowerment. The table lists gains and costs together: recognition and income with a longer working day, and bargaining power with contested earnings. Track three conditions: care shared, earnings in her control and **decent work**. Report total time use too.
notes.83: Rights make gains durable. Each row in the table sets a floor: equal pay law, maternity provision, PoSH, the work guarantee and social protection. A floor is the worst case the law permits. Where a floor is not enforced, **making the claiming mechanism work** often moves more than arguing for a higher floor.
notes.84: The 2017 amendment extended paid leave from 12 to 26 weeks and mandated creches in larger establishments. The catch is reach, since the informal workforce is largely outside it. The employer-borne cost may affect hiring, so the standard answer is to **socialise the cost** through a state-funded benefit.
notes.85: PoSH requires employers to prevent and redress harassment, with Internal Committees and, for small units and informal workers, district Local Committees. The table lists the common gaps. For an employer, **constituting and training an Internal Committee is a checkable statutory duty**.
notes.86: MGNREGA's gender provisions are a third of work for women, equal wages, worksite creches and work close to home. Each can be checked against public muster rolls, which suits social audit. The parenthesis records the repeal from 1 July 2026, so **check the replacement law's rules** before relying on these details.
notes.87: List each instrument with its enrolment condition: work demand, first live birth, enrolment, ration card. Exclusion errors at enrolment fall on the same people across all of them. A woman without documents in her own name misses several at once, so **identity documentation is a WEE issue**.
notes.88: The five rows show rights that exist while the mechanism to claim them does not reach the woman: no pay record, informal employment, no committee, family pressure, unregistered demand. That differs from a weak law. Spend effort on **awareness, documentation and local claiming mechanisms**.
notes.89: A protection whose cost falls on the employer of a woman gives a reason not to employ women. The table pairs three protections with their perverse effect and fix. Keep the right and move the cost: **socialise it or make the requirement universal.**
notes.90: The final test has four questions: is the programme connected to an entitlement, does it build a claiming route, does it reach informal workers and does it survive your exit? Linking a gain to a statutory entitlement turns a project output into **something the state owes**.
notes.92: Empowerment sits inside people's lives, so every indicator is a proxy. Say which proxy you use and what it misses. The table pairs risks and guards. Watch response shift: a programme that changes what a woman considers normal can make **the same answer mean something different at endline**.
notes.93: Read across the table from strong indicator to weak substitute. Household-level figures are available in surveys and hide intra-household inequality. Combine economic measures with agency, control and qualitative voice. For any claim about women, **insist on individual-level measurement**.
notes.94: WEAI measures empowerment across five areas: production, resources, income, leadership and time. It interviews a woman and a man in the same household, so it benchmarks women against the men they live with. Its distinctive feature is the **time measure**, which most empowerment measures omit.
notes.95: Compare the approaches by evidence: cash helps consumption, assets in her name give stronger shifts, credit alone is mixed and graduation bundles are among the most consistent. Bundles cost more per participant, so the choice is fewer participants with a bundle or more with one component. **State which you chose and why.**
notes.96: The heights are illustrative and the message is directional: addressing several constraints at once beats any single lever. Exact effect sizes depend on context. The budget trade is real, so **say whether you reached fewer people properly or more people partially**.
notes.97: 'Women' is not one group. Caste, class, disability, marital status and location compound each constraint. Always disaggregate. Cross at least two axes where the sample allows, and where it does not, **say so** and avoid reporting the aggregate as if it covered everyone.
notes.98: Five principles become five questions: would we do this with no return, which of the three dimensions have we measured, what are we adding to her day, whose name and who decides, and which women? If you carry one, take the fourth, since **many overstated claims report access as a control finding**.
notes.99: Use this page to pick your next reading. Kabeer is the framework at source, Agarwal covers land and bargaining and Elson covers the care Rs. Agarwal's book is theory, so cite it as such. The three Indian data sources are free and current and carry **most of what a WEE argument needs**.
